2	
3	Changesets are structured records of what changed and why, used to generate release notes and communicate changes to consumers.
4	
5	## The changeset@1 Schema
6	
7	```json

9	  "summary": "Add cross-language recon agent to proof plugin",
10	  "files_changed": ["plugins/proof/subagents/recon.md"],
11	  "tests_added": [],
12	  "acceptance_criteria_met": ["SPEC-001-AC-3", "SPEC-001-AC-4"],

15	  "linked_spec": "SPEC-001",
16	  "linked_plan": "PLAN-001"

18	```
19	
20	## Changeset vs. Commit Message
21	
22	- **Commit message**: for developers reading git history. Explains the technical change.
23	- **Changeset summary**: for consumers of the package. Explains the user-visible impact.
24	
25	Same change, two framings:

48	
49	Write a changeset for every PR that:

Closer than it looks — `delta` already delegates to 5 distinct subagents (one per phase), and the "receiving feedback" vs "giving feedback" split already exists conceptually: `delta/review` (`review-preprocessor`) triages *incoming* comments, while *giving* feedback on someone else's PR is actually handled outside delta entirely, by the separate `code-review` skill (`--comment` posts inline PR review comments). So the subagent boundaries are already clean.

The actual smell is one level up: it's a single skill named `ship` with one giant trigger description covering six different verbs (commit, PR, review, changeset, release) crammed into one `SKILL.md`. That risks over-triggering (any mention of "review" or "feedback" fires the whole ship skill) and makes it unclear at a glance which sub-skill applies. I'd lean toward splitting the *skill file* into separate triggerable skills that each still delegate to the existing subagents — not creating new subagents — but the tradeoff is losing the natural "ship this end-to-end" composition (commit → changeset → PR in one request), which a single orchestrating skill handles more gracefully than four independently-triggered ones would.

That's the established convention: one broad-trigger skill per plugin, fanning out to multiple subagents for each phase. `canon` alone spans drafting, auditing, verifying, and gating under a single trigger — same shape as `delta`.

So no, we haven't split any plugin into multiple skills anywhere — `delta` isn't an outlier, it's following the house pattern. If anything, splitting it would be the first deviation from convention, not a correction of one.

That said, your instinct about overloaded triggers isn't wrong in general — a single skill description covering six verbs *can* dilute trigger precision — but the fix this repo has consistently reached for is a **thin dispatcher skill + a strict per-subagent dispatch matrix** (see `delta`'s `<subagent_dispatch_matrix>` table), not multiple skill files. The tradeoff: splitting skills buys sharper individual triggers but costs you the "ship this end-to-end" composition and breaks a pattern six other plugins rely on; keeping one skill with a clean dispatch table keeps composition and consistency but leans on the description being well-scoped.

## Sources & concrete rules

**[Google Developer Documentation Style Guide](https://developers.google.com/style/tone)** — conversational but not dry; second person, active voice, present tense; serial comma; "write for scanning first, being read second" mindset; "sound like a knowledgeable friend," not marketing copy.

**[Microsoft Writing Style Guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/brand-voice-above-all-simple-human)** — 3 principles: warm/relaxed, crisp/clear, ready-to-help. "Crisp and clear" = write for scanning first, reading second. Conciseness rule: no wasted words, no filler qualifiers, be affirmative not hedgy.

**[Diátaxis](https://diataxis.fr/)** — 4 separate doc modes (tutorial / how-to / reference / explanation), each answering a different question. Applies structurally: don't mix "why this works" explanation into a "how to ship a PR" how-to — keep reference (schema/API) separate from narrative (why the change matters).

**[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/)** — fixed categories (Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed/Security); newest-first; "Unreleased" section at top; **write for the reader, not the tracker** — no bare "fixes #123," describe user-visible impact; regular cadence.

**[Federal Plain Language Guidelines](https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/principles)** — active voice always (name who does the action); sentence length target **15–20 words average**; one idea per sentence; cut wordy constructions.

**[NN/G, F-shaped reading pattern](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/f-shaped-pattern-reading-web-content-discovered/)** — users read ~20–28% of on-page text; they scan, not read. Countermeasure: **inverted pyramid** (conclusion first), front-loaded bolded/keyword phrases, short paragraphs, bullets over blocks.

**AI-slop word lists** ([contentbeta](https://www.contentbeta.com/blog/list-of-words-overused-by-ai/), [awesome-slop](https://github.com/hwajongpark/awesome-slop)) — highest-severity terms: *delve, leverage, seamless, robust, elevate, foster, unlock, empower, testament, pivotal, showcase, tapestry, landscape, underscore, meticulous, game-changer, cutting-edge, unprecedented, transformative, utilize (vs "use")*. Also banned structures: "It isn't just X, it's Y," rhetorical-question hooks, triplet-of-adjectives padding.

**LLM anti-slop prompting** ([Anti-Slop Guide](https://cybertronai.github.io/SutroYaro/tooling/anti-slop-guide/), [Towards AI prompt](https://learnaitogethernewsletter.substack.com/p/the-prompt-we-use-to-prevent-ai-slop)) — negative word-bans alone catch ~80% of slop; the rest needs **positive structural constraints** (exact section format, sentence-length ceiling, required front-loaded answer) since a model told only "don't do X" tends to substitute a different flavor of padding. Before/after exemplar pairs outperform abstract rules. A cause worth knowing: RLHF rewards verbose, hedged, enthusiastic-sounding answers — banning words treats the symptom, constraining *structure and length* treats the cause.

## Synthesized guideline set (→ `docs-voice.md`)

1. Lead with the conclusion — answer before justification (inverted pyramid).
2. Active voice, present tense, second person for instructions.
3. One idea per sentence; average sentence length ≤20 words.
4. Bullets/tables over paragraphs whenever the content is enumerable.
5. No banned-word list: *delve, leverage, seamless, robust, elevate, foster, unlock, empower, testament, pivotal, showcase, landscape, underscore, meticulous, game-changer, transformative, utilize→use, dive into*.
6. No rhetorical-question hooks, no "it isn't just X, it's Y," no adjective triplets.
7. State the mechanism, not the adjective — numbers/behavior over "robust"/"powerful" (matches existing `orin-visual-standard.md` §4 rule).
8. Separate *what changed* (reference-like, factual) from *why* (one sentence, no more) — don't blend.
9. Changelog/changeset entries: fixed category, user-facing impact language, no bare issue-number-only lines.
10. PR bodies: summary bullets first, test plan as checklist, no prose recap of the diff.
11. Cut hedge/filler qualifiers ("essentially," "basically," "in order to," "it's worth noting that").
12. Self-edit pass: after drafting, re-read once specifically checking items 5–6 before output — prompt-only banned-word constraints miss ~20% without this.

Good catch — the schema currently has a gap that lets exactly this problem happen. `changeset@1` has no `semver_impact` field at all; the only place `type`/semver shows up is inside `release-artifact@1`, which redeclares a separate mini-changeset shape instead of reusing `changeset@1`. So today, semver classification only happens after the fact, at aggregation time, by `release-summarizer` guessing from a pile of summaries — not per-change, at the point where the diff is actually in front of an agent.

**Proposed redesign:**

1. **`changeset@1` gets two new fields, set by `changeset-analyzer` at creation time:**
   - `consumer_impact`: `behavior-change | new-capability | internal-only` — forces the agent to answer "does anyone outside this repo see this?" before writing prose. `internal-only` changesets get filtered out of release notes automatically instead of `release-summarizer` guessing.
   - `semver_impact`: `major | minor | patch | none` — computed directly from the existing decision table in `changesets.md` (that table already exists, it's just not wired to a field anyone sets).

2. **A changeset *is* the changelog entry.** Drop the duplicate `type` field from `release-artifact@1`'s inline shape; `release-summarizer`'s job becomes: group `changeset@1` objects by `semver_impact`/`consumer_impact`, take the max `semver_impact` across the set as the release's version bump, sort newest-first. Less to reconcile, one schema of record.

3. **Detail scales with `semver_impact`, not written free-hand:**
   - `patch` / `internal-only` → one clause, no elaboration.
   - `minor` → one sentence, optional one-clause why.
   - `major` (breaking) → summary **plus** each `breaking_changes` entry must state old behavior → new behavior → what the caller does about it, in one sentence — not just "removed X."

   This is a judgment rule in the agent prompt, not new schema shape — keeps `breaking_changes` as `string[]`, just tightens what a valid string looks like.

This makes `changeset-analyzer`'s actual job: classify consumer impact → classify semver impact → write at the detail level that impact earns. That's a schema change (`changeset@1`, `release-artifact@1`) plus rewrites to `changeset-analyzer.md` and `release-summarizer.md`, and an update to `changesets.md` to state the table is now machine-enforced, not just guidance.

# Agent Authoring Best Practices

Developer guide for authoring agents, skills, and plugins in this repository. Read this before writing anything. The authoritative rules are in `shared/constitution.md` — this document explains the principles behind them and how to apply them.

---

## 1. The 4-Part Agent Structure

Every agent body uses four named XML sections. This is the only structure — not 5 sections, not a `<role>` block, not a `<success_criteria>` checklist.

```
<load_first>
Read `shared/references/<file>.md` before doing anything else.
[Only present when the agent uses a shared reference file for its phase.]
</load_first>

<backstory>
2–4 sentences of experiential perspective. What has this agent been burned by?
What does it value as a result? This shapes judgment in open situations — it is
not a role label and not a list of responsibilities.
</backstory>

<goal>
What the agent must produce and why. Intent, not steps. One short paragraph.
</goal>

<judgment>
How to know if the goal was genuinely achieved vs. output that merely looks like
it was. Name the key failure mode explicitly. "Did you run the tool or read
mentally?" is a judgment criterion. "Did the spec have no ambiguity?" is not.
</judgment>

<output>
Structured output shape. Reference shared/schemas/<name>@<version>.json when
the output flows to another agent.

EARS notation (WHEN / IF / WHILE / WHERE / THE SYSTEM SHALL) belongs here for:
- Output contracts: WHEN X, THE SYSTEM SHALL produce Y
- Never-do rules: IF Z, the agent SHALL NOT do W
</output>
```

### Why backstory, not role

A role label ("Senior Rust Engineer") tells the model what to pretend to be. A backstory tells the model what it has learned from past failures — and what it therefore values. Backstory shapes judgment in genuinely ambiguous situations. Role shapes posture, which rarely matters.

### Why judgment, not success_criteria

A checklist of success criteria is theater — the agent can tick every box and still produce wrong output. Judgment names the specific way the agent is most likely to fool itself: "did you execute shell commands or read the code mentally?" A good judgment criterion makes the failure mode visible before it happens.

---

## 2. Progressive Context Loading

Agents load only the context they need for their cognitive phase.

```
<load_first>
Read `shared/references/rust-hazards.md` before doing anything else. It contains
the taxonomy definitions and grep patterns for this phase. Do not read
rust-smells.md or rust-tooling.md.
</load_first>
```

**Why this matters:** attention degrades when a context window contains material the agent won't use. A scanner loading all three reference files will pattern-match less precisely than one that loaded only the hazard file. Load exactly one reference file per agent — the one for its cognitive phase.

**Reference file split by concern:**
- `rust-hazards.md` / `typescript-hazards.md` — scanner, adversary, boundary-tracer
- `rust-smells.md` / `typescript-smells.md` — architect
- `rust-tooling.md` / `typescript-tooling.md` — mutator, remediator

---

Agents are dispatched by the cognitive mode they require, not by pipeline position. A scan agent and an analysis agent can run sequentially but must be separate agents because they require different mental modes:

| Mode | What it requires | Agents |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Enumeration | Mechanical completeness, no judgment | recon, scanner |
| Tracing | Systematic data flow following | boundary-tracer |
| Adversarial | Default-to-skepticism, requires concrete failing scenario | adversary |
| Systemic | Cross-finding pattern recognition | architect |
| Behavioral testing | Tool execution and gap identification | mutator |
| Judgment | Weighing competing evidence for a binding decision | exit-gate, verifier |

2	
3	Authoritative rules for all plugins in this repository. EARS-format hard constraints — the fence that all plugin development must stay inside. The interior (how an agent reasons, searches, and decides) is intentionally unconstrained.
4	
5	All rules use EARS notation: WHEN / IF / WHERE / WHILE / THE SYSTEM SHALL.

8

12	```

49

51	
52	WHEN executing shell operations, THE SYSTEM SHALL prioritize modern CLI tools (ripgrep `rg`, `fd`, `bat`, `jq`, `delta`, `eza`) over legacy builtins (`grep`, `find`, `sed`, `cat`).

5	Handles everything after implementation: commit messages, PR descriptions, changeset extraction, review triage, and release notes. It reads the staged diff, linked spec, and linked requirement at runtime to produce meaningful, context-aware output, not mechanical templates.

9	## When to Use

11	- You need a commit message that explains *why*, not just *what*
12	- You're opening a PR and want a description a reviewer with zero context can act on
13	- You need to categorize and respond to PR review comments
14	- You're cutting a release and need user-facing release notes

# graph — Need Definition

**Stage:** Need · **Output:** `requirement@1` · **Version:** 1.0.1

Converts a raw need statement — a one-liner, a vague complaint, a stakeholder ask — into a structured `requirement@1` artifact that a spec writer can act on without asking a single follow-up question. Works with GitHub Issues by default; any issue tracker that emits `requirement@1` can substitute.

---

## When to Use

- You have a fuzzy idea and want to structure it before anyone writes code
- You need to capture a stakeholder request as a formal, traceable requirement
- You want to audit the backlog for gaps, duplicates, or requirements with no matching spec
- You need to link a requirement to related requirements, existing specs, or implementation files

**Invoke with:** `"We need X"`, `"Users are asking for Y"`, `"The problem is Z"`, `"Capture this requirement"`, `"Audit the backlog"`

---

## Sub-skills

| Sub-skill | What it does |
| :--- | :--- |
| `graph/capture` | Converts a free-text need into a `requirement@1` draft — no questions asked, all inferred fields noted |
| `graph/prioritize` | Ranks a set of requirement drafts by impact, urgency, and dependency order |
| `graph/connect` | Links a requirement to related requirements, specs, and implementation files already in the workspace |
| `graph/audit` | Cross-references all open requirements against specs, plans, and implementation files — surfaces gaps, coverage, and duplicates |

---

## Subagents

| Subagent | Role | Tier | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `intake` | Intake Structurer | sonnet / medium | Converts free text into a `requirement@1` draft. Infers all fields it can; leaves gaps noted in `reasoning`. |
| `clarifier` | Clarifier | sonnet / medium | Identifies the most critical gap in the draft and asks one focused question, or returns the completed requirement if all dimensions are met. |
| `auditor` | Auditor | sonnet / medium | Cross-references a completed `requirement@1` against stated stakeholder needs to confirm it is complete and internally consistent. |

---

## Pipeline

```
[free text] → intake → clarifier (× N) → auditor → requirement@1
```

The clarifier loops until each `done_when` criterion is specific enough to write a failing test against it, the stakeholder is identified with enough context, and `out_of_scope` boundaries are explicit.

---

## Output Schema

`requirement@1` — see `shared/schemas/requirement@1.json`

| Field | Required | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `id` | yes | Unique requirement identifier |
| `statement` | yes | One sentence describing the need |
| `stakeholder` | yes | Who this serves, with enough context to understand their perspective |
| `why` | yes | Underlying pain or opportunity |
| `done_when` | yes | Array of testable propositions, each confirmable true/false from the outside |
| `out_of_scope` | yes | Explicit boundaries that prevent scope creep |
| `reasoning` | yes | Scratchpad — never forwarded downstream |

A requirement is complete when a downstream spec writer can read it and produce an accurate, unambiguous spec without asking clarifying questions.

---

## Install

**Claude Code** — add the marketplace once, then install by ID:
```
/plugin marketplace add orin-dx/agent-plugins
/plugin install graph
```

**AGY** — installs the full repo; see the [root README](../../README.md#quick-start) for instructions.

---

## Next Stage

Feed `requirement@1` to **[trace](../trace/)** for research, or directly to **[canon](../canon/)** if no prior art survey is needed.

---

## Extensibility

Any issue tracker (Jira, Linear, Notion) can substitute as the backing store as long as it emits `requirement@1`. The downstream pipeline is agnostic — it only consumes the schema.

# basis — Plugin Authoring

**Stage:** Meta · **Output:** conformant plugin directory · **Version:** 1.0.1

The tool for building tools. Scaffolds new plugins, audits existing ones for ecosystem conformance, and designs inter-agent JSON schema contracts. Output from `scaffolder` is a ready-to-install plugin directory — `plugin.json`, `SKILL.md`, stub subagents, and the `shared` symlink already wired.

---

## When to Use

- You want to build a new plugin and need the correct directory structure
- You've written a plugin and want to verify it conforms to ecosystem rules
- You need to design a new JSON schema for a new inter-agent artifact type
- You want to generate a single conformant subagent `.md` file for an existing plugin

**Invoke with:** `"Create a plugin called X that does Y"`, `"Audit the X plugin for conformance"`, `"Design a schema for an artifact that carries Z"`, `"Write a subagent for task T at opus/high tier"`

---

## Sub-skills

| Sub-skill | What it does |
| :--- | :--- |
| `basis/scaffold` | Generates a complete, ready-to-install plugin directory given a plugin ID and description |
| `basis/audit` | Audits an existing plugin directory against all ecosystem conformance rules; returns structured pass/fail/warn per check |
| `basis/schema` | Designs a new JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for an inter-agent artifact; checks for conflicts with existing schemas |
| `basis/subagent` | Generates a single conformant subagent `.md` file using the 4-part structure |

---

## Subagents

| Subagent | Role | Tier | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `scaffolder` | Scaffolder | sonnet / medium | Generates a complete plugin directory: `plugin.json`, `SKILL.md`, stub subagents, `shared` symlink. |
| `auditor` | Conformance Auditor | sonnet / medium | Audits a plugin directory for ecosystem conformance across all required fields, structure rules, and authoring principles. |
| `schema-designer` | Schema Designer | sonnet / medium | Designs a new JSON Schema for a proposed inter-agent artifact; checks for conflicts with existing schemas. |

---

## Conformance Checks (auditor)

The auditor checks all of the following. A plugin that fails any check is not ecosystem-conformant:

| Check | Rule |
| :--- | :--- |
| Manifest fields | `plugin.json` has all required fields: `id`, `name`, `version`, `description`, `author`, `skills`, `agents` |
| Skill file | `skills/<id>/SKILL.md` exists with valid YAML frontmatter and a `description` trigger string |
| Agent files | All agents listed in `plugin.json` have a corresponding `.md` file |
| Agent descriptions | 80–200 words each; start with "Delegate to this subagent when…" |
| 4-part body structure | Agent body has exactly: backstory, goal, judgment, output — no success_criteria, no role sections, EARS only in output |
| Model/effort tiering | Mechanical → haiku/low; Analysis → sonnet/medium; Judgment → opus/high |
| `shared` symlink | Points to `../../shared` — never copied or embedded |
| No authoring-time refs | Agent bodies do not reference `shared/agent-best-practices.md` at runtime |

---

## Directory Layout

Plugins produced by `scaffolder` follow this exact layout:

```
plugins/<id>/
├── plugin.json                  # id, name, version, description, author, skills, agents
├── shared -> ../../shared       # symlink — never copy
├── skills/
│   └── <id>/
│       └── SKILL.md             # YAML frontmatter + body
└── agents/
    └── <agent-name>.md          # one file per agent in plugin.json
```

---

## Key Authoring Principles

basis enforces these conventions when scaffolding and auditing:

- **Pull over inject** — agents receive a workspace path and a goal; they discover what they need via tools
- **Goal over procedure** — prompts express the desired outcome, not step-by-step scripts
- **Minimum viable prompt** — body target under 200 words; role + goal + output shape + a few heuristics
- **Self-contained** — prompts run identically on Claude Code and AGY; no runtime ...

1	# Documentation Voice Reference
2	
3	Canonical voice standard for this repo: commit messages, PR bodies, changesets, release notes, and prose docs (READMEs, `basis`-scaffolded plugin docs). Succinct, engineering-focused, scannable. No AI slop.
4	
5	Agents load only the subset embedded in their own task reference file (`conventional-commits.md`, `github.md`, `changesets.md`) — see each for the operational rules. This file is the full standard, for humans and for `basis` when scaffolding new docs.
6	
7	## Rules
8	
9	1. Lead with the conclusion. Answer before justification (inverted pyramid) — readers scan ~20-28% of page text, they don't read top to bottom.
10	2. Active voice, present tense, second person for instructions.
11	3. One idea per sentence. Average sentence length ≤20 words.
12	4. Bullets or tables over paragraphs whenever the content is enumerable.
13	5. Separate *what changed* (factual, reference-like) from *why* (one sentence, no more) — don't blend them into one block.
14	6. State the mechanism, not the adjective. Numbers and behavior over "robust" / "powerful" / "seamless."
15	7. Cut hedge and filler qualifiers: "essentially," "basically," "in order to," "it's worth noting that."
16	8. Self-edit pass: after drafting, re-read once checking rules 5 and 9 specifically before output. Banned-word avoidance alone misses ~20% of slop without this pass.
17	
18	## Banned words and phrases
19	
20	*delve, leverage, seamless, robust, elevate, foster, unlock, empower, testament, pivotal, showcase, tapestry, landscape, underscore, meticulous, game-changer, cutting-edge, unprecedented, transformative, utilize (use "use"), dive into, supercharge, empowers, elevate*
21	
22	Banned structures: "It isn't just X, it's Y." Rhetorical-question hooks. Triplets of adjectives as padding.
23	
24	## Review-feedback vocabulary
25	
26	When a change involves triaging or drafting comments on someone else's work (not narrating your own diff), prefix intent so it reads unambiguously before tone does. Two equivalent vocabularies — pick one per context and stay consistent within it:
27	
28	- **Conventional Comments**: `praise:` `nitpick:` `suggestion:` `issue:` `question:` `thought:` — optionally decorated `(non-blocking)`.
29	- **Google code review style**: `Nit:` `Optional:` / `Consider:` `FYI:` for anything that isn't a blocking request.

5	This document defines the quantitative visualization standards, color palettes, typography, and human-computer interaction (HCI) rules governing `lumen-cli` and `Lumen for Mac`.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. Foundational Design Principles
10	
11	Lumen adheres to the rigorous visual display principles established by **Edward Tufte**, **Stephen Few**, **Ben Shneiderman**, and **Colin Ware**:
12	
13	```text
14	┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
15	│                        DATA PRESENTATION DESIGN SYSTEM                                 │
16	├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
17	│  1. SHNEIDERMAN'S MANTRA: Overview First ➔ Zoom & Filter ➔ Details-on-Demand           │
18	│  2. TUFTE'S DATA-INK MAXIMIZATION: Eliminate chartjunk; use inline sparklines          │
19	│  3. FEW'S DENSE BULLET GRAPHS: Replace round gauges with compact threshold bars        │
20	│  4. PREATTENTIVE COLOR ENCODING (Ware): Semantic color only for anomalies & state      │
21	│  5. ZERO-MENTAL-MATH NUMBER FORMATTING: Always pair raw counts with financial context  │
22	└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
23	```
24

26	
27	## 2. Preattentive Semantic Palette
28	
29	Human visual perception decodes contrast and color in **`< 200ms`**. To minimize cognitive fatigue:
30	* **Muted Neutral Slate Chrome (90% of screen)**: Charcoal, slate, and off-white for borders, headers, labels, and standard turn rows.

2	
3	This guide provides instructions, architectural rules, engineering invariants, and task runner workflows for AI coding agents (Antigravity, Claude, Cursor, Copilot, Codex) working on the Lumen codebase.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Repository Architecture & Crate Layers
8	
9	Lumen is a multi-orchestrator telemetry, session intelligence, and token economics engine written in Rust. It is structured into strict architectural layers:
10	
11	```text
12	┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
13	│                          LUMEN CRATE LAYERS                            │
14	├───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┤
15	│ LAYER & CRATE                     │ LICENSE & PURPOSE                  │
16	├───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
17	│ Layer 1: lumen-model              │ MIT / Apache-2.0                   │
18	│                                   │ Canonical IR & Pricing Matrix      │
19	├───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
20	│ Layer 1.5: lumen-session          │ MIT / Apache-2.0                   │
21	│                                   │ Streaming Ingestion & Adapters     │
22	├───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
23	│ Layer 2: lumen-analysis           │ FSL-1.1-MIT                        │
24	│          lumen-pattern            │ 22 Accumulators, Trajectory DAG    │
25	├───────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
26	│ Layer 4: lumen-cli                │ FSL-1.1-MIT                        │
27	│                                   │ Standalone CLI & Telemetry Tools   │
28	└───────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
29	```
30	
31	> **CRITICAL RULE (Layer Licensing Boundaries)**: Layer 1 (`lumen-model`) and Layer 1.5 (`lumen-session`) MUST NOT depend on Layer 2 or Layer 4 crates (`lumen-analysis`, `lumen-pattern`, `lumen-cli`). Layer 1/1.5 crates must remain permissive (`MIT OR Apache-2.0`) and standalone.
32	
33	---
34	
35	## 2. Primary Task Runners & Verification Pipelines
36	
37	Always use `just` or `moon` task runners for building, testing, linting, and formatting.
38	
39	| Action | Primary Task Runner Command | Moon Engine Command |
40	| :--- | :--- | :--- |
41	| **Run Full Verification CI** | `just ci` | `moon run :format-check && moon run :lint && moon run :test` |
42	| **Run Test Suite** | `just test` | `moon run :test` |
43	| **Check Clippy Lints** | `just lint` | `moon run :lint` |
44	| **Check Formatting** | `just fmt-check` | `moon run :format-check` |
45	| **Format Code** | `just fmt` | `moon run :format` |
46

49	## 3. Strict Engineering Invariants
50	
51	1. **Safe Rust Only (`unsafe_code = "forbid"`)**: `unsafe` code blocks are strictly forbidden across all workspace crates.
52	2. **Deterministic Token Accounting**: Token calculations must account for uncached input, 5m ephemeral write, 1h write, 0.10x cache read discount, and output tokens without division by zero.
53	3. **Linear Streaming Pass $O(N)$**: Telemetry accumulators must operate in a single linear pass over the canonical turns without nested heap allocations.
54	4. **Tarjan SCC Cycle Detection**: Cycle depth $\ge 3$ on identical target symbols with zero mutation must be flagged as circular loops.
55	5. **Rich Diagnostic Cards (`miette`)**: User-facing CLI errors must derive `miette::Diagnostic`.

# Contributing to Lumen

Contributions to Lumen are welcome. This guide outlines the development environment setup, architectural invariants, and testing standards.

---

## 1. Development Environment

### Prerequisites
- **Rust Toolchain**: Rust 1.80+ (`stable`)
- **Cargo Tools**: `cargo-clippy`, `cargo-fmt`
- **Preferred CLI Tools**: `eza`, `bat`, `ripgrep`, `fd`

### Build and Test

```bash
# Build the workspace
cargo build --workspace

# Run all unit and integration tests
cargo test --workspace

# Check formatting
cargo fmt --all -- --check

# Check clippy lints
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

---

## 2. Engineering Invariants

Contributors must maintain the following architectural rules:

1. **Safe Rust Only (`unsafe_code = "forbid"`)**: Memory and concurrency safety are guaranteed by safe Rust abstractions.
2. **Single-Pass $O(N)$ Processing**: Accumulators in `lumen-analysis` must operate in a single linear pass over the message stream with zero heap allocations in inner loops.
3. **Cumulative Snapshot Merge Invariant**: Context compaction snapshots must always be merged using component-wise $\max()$, never `sum()`.
4. **Permissive Layer 1 Isolation**: Layer 1 crates (`lumen-model`, `lumen-session`) must remain permissive (`MIT OR Apache-2.0`) and must not depend on Layer 2 or Layer 4 crates.
5. **No Emojis or Filler Phrases**: Documentation, commit messages, and diagnostic output must remain technical, concise, and scannable.

---

## 3. Pull Request Workflow

1. **Create a Branch**: Use a descriptive branch name (e.g. `feat/new-accumulator`, `fix/agy-parser`).
2. **Write Tests First**: Add unit or integration tests verifying the change.
3. **Verify CI**: Ensure `cargo test --workspace` and `cargo clippy` pass with zero warnings.
4. **Conventional Commits**: Format commit messages using conventional prefixes (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`).

`axiom` is a reusable, artifact-agnostic verification gate. Any artifact type — spec, plan, changeset, finding report — can be run through it.

        direction LR

        sonnet / medium"] --> Gate["exit-gate
        opus / high"]
    end

    Art --> Recon

    Fix["producing agent
    targeted patch on blockers

    Gate -->|pass| Done(["verdict@1 · pass"])
    Gate -->|fail| Fix
    Fix -->|"retry ≤ 3 · updated retry_count"| Art

On `fail`, the orchestrator passes **only the blockers array** back to the producing agent — not the full artifact context — so it can make a targeted fix. On retry 2, the effort level escalates. After 3 retries, the circuit breaks and control passes to the human.

`retry_count` is tracked inside `verdict@1` and incremented by the exit gate on each pass.

# GitHub Issue Forms YAML Syntax

## Top-Level Keys

The required structure begins with three mandatory keys:

```yaml
name:
description:
body:
```

**Complete top-level key reference:**

| Key | Purpose | Required | Type |
|-----|---------|----------|------|
| `name` | "A name for the issue form template. Must be unique from all other templates" | Yes | String |
| `description` | "A description for the issue form template, which appears in the template chooser interface" | Yes | String |
| `body` | "Definition of the input types in the form" | Yes | Array |
| `title` | "A default title that will be pre-populated in the issue submission form" | No | String |
| `labels` | "Labels that will automatically be added to issues created with this template" | No | Array/String |
| `assignees` | "People who will be automatically assigned to issues created with this template" | No | Array/String |
| `type` | "The issue type that will be automatically added to issues created with this template" | No | String |
| `projects` | Projects for auto-addition (format: `PROJECT-OWNER/PROJECT-NUMBER`) | No | Array/String |

## Supported Body Element Types

### Markdown
```yaml
- type: markdown
  attributes:
    value: |
      [content here]
```

### Input
```yaml
- type: input
  id: [identifier]
  attributes:
    label: [label text]
    description: [helper text]
    placeholder: [placeholder text]
    value: [default value]
  validations:
    required: [true/false]
```

### Textarea
```yaml
- type: textarea
  id: [identifier]
  attributes:
    label: [label text]
    description: [helper text]
    placeholder: [placeholder text]
    value: [default value]
    render: [shell/markdown]
  validations:
    required: [true/false]
```

### Dropdown
```yaml
- type: dropdown
  id: [identifier]
  attributes:
    label: [label text]
    description: [helper text]
    options:
      - [option 1]
      - [option 2]
    default: [index number]
    multiple: [true/false]
  validations:
    required: [true/false]
```

### Checkboxes
```yaml
- type: checkboxes
  id: [identifier]
  attributes:
    label: [label text]
    description: [helper text]
    options:
      - label: [option text]
        required: [true/false]
```

### Upload
```yaml
- type: upload
  id: [identifier]
  attributes:
    label: [label text]
    description: [helper text]
  validations:
    required: [true/false]
```

# YAML Syntax for config.yml

Based on the documentation, here's the exact syntax for `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml`:

## Key Structure

The configuration file uses two main elements:

**blank_issues_enabled**: A boolean setting that controls whether users can create issues without a template. Setting it to `false` restricts blank issues to users with write access or above.

**contact_links**: An array of contact link objects, each containing:
- `name`: The display name for the link
- `url`: The destination URL
- `about`: A description of the link's purpose

## Complete Example

```yaml
blank_issues_enabled: false
contact_links:
  - name: GitHub Community Support
    url: https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions
    about: Please ask and answer questions here.
  - name: GitHub Security Bug Bounty
    url: https://bounty.github.com/
    about: Please report security vulnerabilities here.
```

This configuration "will customize the template chooser when the file is merged into the repository's default branch."

## Overview

You can add default community health files to a public repository called .github and GitHub will use and display default files for any repository owned by the account that does not have its own file of that type.

2	
3	## Reporting a Vulnerability
4	
5	Email **security@orin-dx.com** — don't open a public issue for anything that could be exploited before a fix ships.
6	
7	Include:
8	- Which crate or code path is affected
9	- The concrete failure scenario — what an attacker could do, and how
10	- Steps to reproduce, if you have them
11	
12	Expect an acknowledgment within 5 business days. We'll keep you posted as a fix moves through triage, and credit you in the release notes unless you'd rather stay anonymous.
13	
14	## Scope
15	
16	Callisto edits manifests and pushes releases across multiple package registries from inside CI, so the threat model is higher-stakes than a typical CLI tool:
17	
18	- **Registry token exposure** — Callisto's own release workflow (`.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml`) runs with `contents: write`, `pull-requests: write`, and holds `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN`/`NPM_TOKEN` secrets. A way to make Callisto (or a workflow using `orin-dx/callisto-action`) exfiltrate those tokens, or publish to a package other than the one it was asked to, is a critical finding.
19	- **Workflow/action injection** — Callisto is designed to run unattended on `push` to `main` in downstream repos. An untrusted PR that could get its content executed by the release workflow (rather than merely analyzed) is in scope.
20	- **Manifest parser safety** — `callisto-manifests` edits `Cargo.toml`/`package.json` via CST-preserving parsers (`toml_edit`, `serde_json`) rather than regex specifically to avoid corruption; a crafted manifest that causes incorrect writes, path traversal, or a crash mid-write (bypassing the atomic `NamedTempFile` + `fs::rename` guarantee) is a real finding.
21	- **Version/changelog spoofing** — a way to make `callisto version` compute or apply an incorrect bump, or inject arbitrary content into a generated changelog, that a maintainer could plausibly merge without noticing.
22	- **Git operation safety** — `callisto-vcs` performs native in-process Git operations via `gix`; unsafe handling of an untrusted repository (submodules, refs, hooks) is in scope.
23	
24	Dependency vulnerabilities are already checked continuously via `just audit` (`cargo deny check advisories`) in CI — a report that only restates an existing advisory `cargo audit`/`cargo deny` already flags isn't a new finding, but a way to bypass or disable that check is.
25	
26	Out of scope: vulnerabilities in Cargo, npm, PyPI, or GitHub Actions themselves — report those to the respective platform.
27	
28	## Supported Versions
29	
30	Security fixes land on `main` and the latest published release of each affected crate. Given Callisto is pre-1.0 (`0.3.3`), older minor versions are not backported — upgrade to the latest release.

Is it always one changeset per topic or can related things go into a changeset, it's a bit nebulous on purpose and why AI is good for this right?

Not always 1:1 — related things should absolutely stay in one changeset. The rule I wrote already draws that line: "added X *and* its tests" is one changeset (the tests share X's cause — they exist *because of* X); "added X and *also* fixed unrelated Y" is two (Y would have happened, or not, regardless of X). The test isn't "how many topics" or "how many files" — it's "do these share a cause." A feature plus the refactor it required plus its tests is one coherent story even touching a dozen files; two one-line fixes in the same file for unrelated reasons are two changesets even though they'd look identical to a file-count or commit-count heuristic.

That's exactly why it has to stay judgment rather than becoming a mechanical rule, and it's the same reasoning this whole repo already runs on — the constitution's own line is "EARS is the fence, backstory and goal fill the interior with judgment," and "over-constraining the interior caps the agent at the level of the author's imagination." A rule like "split by commit boundary" or "split by directory" is easy to write and mechanically checkable, but it's *wrong* in exactly the cases that matter: it'll fuse two unrelated one-line fixes that happen to touch the same file, and it'll fragment one real feature across the five files it legitimately needed to touch. Telling "shares a cause" from "coincidentally adjacent" requires actually understanding *why* a change was made, not just what changed — that's a reading-comprehension problem, not a diffing problem, which is the specific thing an LLM can do that a script splitting by file/commit/directory can't. It's also exactly why `callisto`'s own workflow has a changeset *wizard* instead of an auto-splitter — the tool that owns this exact problem professionally still treats it as something requiring a judgment call at authoring time, not something inferable from diff syntax alone.

Say we're doing a push for testing coverage improvement across all packages, that can go in one changeset. Say we're implementing a set of new features together, that can be a changeset.

Agentic work makes this a bit more difficult because the agents do a lot more work quicker, right

Both examples are real, and they show my "shared cause" framing was too narrow — it implied a causal/dependency relationship (X requires Y), but relatedness can also come from **shared deliberate intent** with no causal link at all: a coordinated testing-coverage push across unrelated packages isn't one package's tests requiring another's, it's one *decision* executed across many places. A themed batch of features is the same shape — the features don't depend on each other, but someone chose to scope and ship them as one unit. The real test isn't "does A require B," it's "would a consumer reading release notes understand these as one thing someone decided to do, or as two coincidences that happened to land in the same diff." Cause is one way to get there; a stated, deliberate scope is another.

On agentic velocity making this harder — yes, and I think it's specifically this: a human's commit history naturally encodes intent structure for free (they context-switch, write a commit message reflecting what they were thinking *at that moment*, take breaks between concerns). An agent executing a big plan in one continuous run doesn't have that pacing signal — fifty files touched in one session can be one coordinated effort or three unrelated ones, and the raw diff looks equally dense either way. Volume erases the cue that used to make relatedness obvious.

But this repo's own pipeline actually has a better signal available than most projects do, and I don't think `changeset-analyzer` is told to use it yet: `linked_spec`/`linked_plan`/`linked_requirement`, plus lambda's `covers_criteria`/`criteria_evidence`, are a *recorded* scoping decision — someone (human or agent) already decided "these acceptance criteria belong to this one spec" at planning time, before any code existed. That's a more reliable "shared intent" signal than reconstructing it after the fact from diff prose, because it isn't being inferred, it's being read. Right now the agent's judgment leans entirely on the diff-reading "and" test; it should prefer spec/plan boundaries as the primary signal when they exist, and only fall back to diff-based judgment when nothing was linked at all — which would directly cover your testing-push and feature-batch cases whenever they trace to one spec, and give a real, checkable reason instead of a vibe.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# For each plugin, checks that plugin.json's version, the README's
# **Version:** line, the CHANGELOG's top entry, and marketplace.json's
# per-plugin version all agree. These four are updated by hand on every
# bump and have drifted before (fixed across 4 plugins in v3.1.0) —
# nothing structural stopped it from happening again.
#
# Usage: scripts/check-versions.sh

set -euo pipefail
script_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
# shellcheck source=lib/report.sh
source "$script_dir/lib/report.sh"
cd "$script_dir/.."

fail=0
count=0

for plugin_json in plugins/*/plugin.json; do
  dir="$(dirname "$plugin_json")"
  id="$(basename "$dir")"
  count=$((count + 1))

  pj_version="$(jq -r '.version' "$plugin_json")"
  readme_version="$(grep -oE '\*\*Version:\*\* *[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' "$dir/README.md" | head -1 | grep -oE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' || true)"
  changelog_version="$(grep -oE '^## \[[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' "$dir/CHANGELOG.md" | head -1 | grep -oE '[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+' || true)"
  marketplace_version="$(jq -r --arg id "$id" '.plugins[] | select(.id == $id) | .version' marketplace.json)"

  mismatches=()
  [[ -z "$readme_version" ]] && mismatches+=("README: no **Version:** line found")
  [[ -n "$readme_version" && "$readme_version" != "$pj_version" ]] && mismatches+=("README says $readme_version")
  [[ -z "$changelog_version" ]] && mismatches+=("CHANGELOG: no ## [x.y.z] entry found")
  [[ -n "$changelog_version" && "$changelog_version" != "$pj_version" ]] && mismatches+=("CHANGELOG says $changelog_version")
  [[ -z "$marketplace_version" ]] && mismatches+=("marketplace.json: no entry for id \"$id\"")
  [[ -n "$marketplace_version" && "$marketplace_version" != "$pj_version" ]] && mismatches+=("marketplace.json says $marketplace_version")

  if [[ ${#mismatches[@]} -gt 0 ]]; then
    fail=$((fail + 1))
    echo "FAIL: $id (plugin.json: $pj_version)"
    for m in "${mismatches[@]}"; do
      echo "    $m"
    done
  fi
done

report_check "$fail" "$count" \
  "plugin(s), all versions agree across plugin.json/README/CHANGELOG/marketplace.json." \
  "plugin(s) have version drift. Fix and re-run."

On markdown formatting — worth separating **formatter** (auto-rewrites content) from **linter** (flags, doesn't touch content). A formatter is riskier here: most markdown formatters default to reflowing prose at a column width, which directly violates your standing "never hard-wrap" rule unless configured carefully (e.g. Prettier's `proseWrap: preserve`). A linter (`markdownlint-cli2` via `npx`, check-only, same on-demand pattern as `check-mermaid.sh`) fits better — it flags real inconsistencies (heading levels, list markers, trailing whitespace) without rewriting prose, and matches the check-don't-fix philosophy already used for the three scripts we just built.

Recommend: `markdownlint-cli2` in check mode, `MD013` (line-length) disabled explicitly so it can never conflict with the no-wrap rule. Want me to set that up?
I think that would be good. Any alternatives that might be better?

Three real alternatives, differing in what they actually check:

- **markdownlint-cli2** — structure only (heading levels, list markers, whitespace). npx-based, no new dependency type, same precedent as `check-mermaid.sh`. Lowest friction, but this repo hasn't actually had structural markdown bugs.
- **Prettier `--check`** — similar structural scope plus auto-fix, but normalizes more (emphasis markers, table alignment) — higher risk of a noisy, invasive diff across ~50 existing files on first run.
- **Vale** — a prose linter, not a structure linter. It can directly enforce `docs-voice.md`'s banned-word list (*delve, leverage, seamless...*) and voice rules — the thing that's actually been manually eyeballed all session and is the repo's real documented pain point. Tradeoff: it's a Go binary (brew/curl install), not npx — breaks the "no new dependency type" precedent the other three scripts share.

The structural tools solve a problem this repo doesn't really have yet; Vale solves one it already has and has a rule file for. Worth doing both, or just Vale first?
